scores.why: Big flat oxblood polygons with bone needle tips are a real picture, close to Kandinsky's hard shapes, and the "thinnest needle is gone first" rule is seen, not explained. A repeat that re-sharpens a pebble in one step is the best moment. The risk is the frame after a second: a scatter of dim round pebbles, and a spiked polygon can look like a comic-book star if the tips are too even.

You can count tiers with a finger and the whole past jumps on each note, with "zero overshoot, zero easing". It has an Ikeda barcode feel with a red cap on top, which this user likes. But on a still frame it is a bar chart, the body sits at T 0.22 to 0.38, and the eye sees striped bars more than needles.

An undrawn black slab known only by a comb of parallel needles is a strong graphic idea, and "every tenth 60..160 px" gives the comb a real bristle. Chords cutting into each other's combs would look like an engraving. In slow music it is a flash and then a few spines, so the frame is mostly black, and pitch is hard to read from a golden-ratio x.

Three angles only, T-junctions only, and two ends, blunt where stopped and hair-fine where it ran out. That builds a constructivist picture that stands for seconds and looks like nothing else here. Oxblood at T 0.25 to 0.4 is the low end of what will read, so `weight` must stay heavy, or it slides toward cracked glass and the shatter verdict.

A huge dark-red hexagon with a razor line is the snap-squares weight this user liked, and the same note is always the same seam. But it has only a dozen sheets, each moved by a few px, and "no surface detail", so most frames are a slightly stepped polygon. Rigid is there, but it is little to look at for a whole clip.

An interval as "the angle between textures" is clever, and the snap is perfect because the fade does everything. On the frame, though, it is scattered short dashes with no form, the essay's own "N particles" worry. The eye gets confetti and needs to be told about the angle.

Broad toothed bands of oxblood pile crossing on black, with crossings cut out by evenodd, are Kline in velvet and a picture you would hang. A viewer says "velvet" unprompted, and "the velvet itself is never drawn" is a real decision. The on, off, on repeat is countable but can read as a note removing itself, and large pattern fills every step need testing beside other widgets.

The seam made only by two copies of fur disagreeing is a lovely trick, and the fur would read at once. But a patch of hide that shakes at 14 Hz, "fuzziest when moving", is a trembling body, the exact thing the user recoiled from. Pitch is only which patch, so a melody is hard to follow.

Near-black Miró shapes with all the light in a rim of separate hairs, Oppenheim's fur cup on a black stage, is the strongest pure texture in the set: you would say fur before anything else. Hair stands straight out on a repeat and lies down in three stepped stances. After the flash it is a dim nap around a dark shape, and the six outlines must stay signs, because furry blobs can turn into cute creatures or something bodily very quickly.

Clumped teeth with a shared tip are well observed, and the tips sweeping an arc as they lie down is nice. But the frame is one thin line with a patch of spikes, too near a spectrum meter and to Ridges. It is too little picture for 1280 by 720.

A row of hard brushes could look like a Klee line drawing, and repeats as closed identical brushes count well. But the main decision, fan width from "the melody's curvature", has to be explained to be seen, and a row of tufts on a bent line is a caterpillar. The rigid-on-elastic texture only lasts through a 0.2 s wag.

Lobed acid-green moss patches on black are a picture of moss, and a soft dome with a dent and a dense bright lip is the suggestive shape the essay admits to. The wet-to-dry colour memory is the good part. The attack itself is small next to a 460 px cushion, so the note is under-served.

Mustard and rust colonies with black gutters could end as a handsome Klee map, and repeats building a finger "one knuckle at a time" is memorable. But a lobe is a small event, with low snap, and the picture is about the accumulated map rather than the note. Rounded growing blobs with a crust can also read as mould on a dish.

Power-law sizes and clumps, with "a dozen big shards", give this a scale from across the room that Glint lacks, and the identical constellation on a repeat is recognised as the ear recognises it. Not a pixel moves and it is seek-exact. It is still scatter with no form, attractive for a moment and then a question of what it is a picture of.

The tilted packages cut by a flat bed, with a silence as a visible event landing on a note, would be a stunning still in earth tones. Thickness from time to the next chord is the kind of thing a musician notices. But it risks "explaining how it works", as the essay says, and it is a chart of history. The grain is too fine to carry the texture.

Sharpness earned by subtraction, repeats leaving needle cusps you can count, is a great idea. But the default stone is (40, 34, 44) at T 0.3, which is effectively invisible on black, and the silhouette is the entire record. This is the Blade failure unless the oxblood colour becomes the default.

A huge dark slab that shears like "a deck pushed from the side", where the flash decays into a black crack in the same pixel. Registers the melody lives in shear into thin leaves "with no code for it", so the frame gets richer as the song goes. It is a flat form with a stepped edge and very close to what this user liked last night.

Dark polygons with lit rims on near-black (28, 24, 30) walls are a low-contrast window of Cells, with depth doing what a brighter tile did. The circle-of-fifths map is a thing you are told. The refusal to ripple is honest, but the eye sees a dim mosaic, and rigid here is only stillness.

"The flash is the cell, the note has an area" gives big flat red planes and a hard line in the same step, which reads strongly, near Boogie Woogie and LeWitt. The narrowing-ladder repeat is good. But recursive subdivision is a well-worn generative look and it says Mondrian, not rigid or sharp, and the settled lines are only ash.

Cadmium orange on black is the boldest colour in the set, and nested terraces count repeats well. "A note emits nothing" is a nice thought, and the oxidising fall is purely downward. The essay admits it is the one closest to its subject, and 30 jigsaw plates in three rows with grey ground says pine bark.

Cream strips with a salmon underside and a small scroll at the end are charming, a typographer's swash. It risks being decorative, and the spiral is only 14 px on a frame where the strip is 700. Pitch is just a row, and the bigger curl gesture is better done by Snapweed.

The most original concept here: a thread thinning as `(time left)^(2/3)` so the note is the break. But a bud growing where the next note will land is a visible event with no note, and the essay itself worries about "two round masses and a shaft". On screen it is close to Honey too, and this user would likely call it too suggestive before seeing the law.

A ruled bone bar that "cannot stay a bar", turning into dots at spacing 4.5h, so loud means few and fat and soft means many and fine. Rows of dots are Kusama and Ikeda together, a real signature. The elastic part lasts a tenth of a second, and after that it is dotted lines, so the claimed texture is seen only briefly.

A dark-red slab torn open with an edge-to-edge comb of bone hourglass fibres, fuzz that exists only because something is being stretched. "Regular in spacing and random in failure" is exactly the observed thing, and it gives no front. It sits next to the snap squares the user liked and adds a texture you feel in the teeth. Watch that a horizontal seam with strands does not read as a mouth.

One large flat ink-blue sail with scooped edges closing to needles is a complete picture on every frame, as if Kandinsky drew a stretched skin. You see taut before you know why, since the edges are "drum-tight at the blow" and slacken into scoops. Each new note is one bright tip, and the corners are always the last three notes. Blue also breaks the oxblood monotony of the whole set.

A disc with a hard rim at a point, shrinking, is the dropped ripples turned inside out, and loud notes become cogs, which are mechanical, not elastic. The fixed contact time is a fact nobody will see on a screen with many notes. Flat ultramarine discs are pleasant but close to Delaunay and Kusama.

A dead-straight line for 33 ms and then its own slack as a smooth scribble is a marvellous gesture, and it leaves Twombly marks nobody drew. Elastic is unmistakable. It is thin, though: the settled squiggles are 2 px and small, and repeats are told apart only by a new scribble on the same line.

A run that cuts a lane through a pelt so "passages become places" is the good part. But most of the time it is dim static at 30 % with holes, and a round rim around each hole is close to the banned ring from a point. A history-dependent layer also costs seek exactness.

A skin that shows only where it bends is elegant: nested V cusps floating on black like fletching, with "flat is invisible". But hairlines with alpha following slope are thin and quickly faint, so it may be too dim to carry beside other widgets, and the width never changes with the note. Nested Vs converging on a point need checking for moiré and for what they suggest.

Pitch as leverage is a great physical idea: a bass note throws 1700 px of line and treble flicks the tip. But a shaft with barbs every 5 px is a drawing of a feather, however long, and at T 0.3 it is a faint one. The jolt would be thrilling, yet what stands there is a thin barbed zigzag.

The crowded flanks, "denser than the untouched surface", are lovely observation and the flat oxblood sheet looks rich. But a V opening in a hairy sheet with bright flanks that slowly closes is the same image Essay 2 threw out as Parting. The diagonal helps, but this user has a word for it.

A 520 px bone needle that is a clock spring three steps later, then "spent". The marks come out as Miró curlicues with a true point, and a row of hooks is a frieze you want to look at. Elastic with no return is a fresh idea, though tall strips standing from the floor must never be seen upright for long, and a page of them can drift toward art nouveau ferns.

The 1.5-node tooth that makes the hatch "twice as fine" for a moment, so speed turns rigid into fuzz, is the cleverest use of the canvas fade in any essay. But it is 1 px dark straw at about T 0.2, so the ground is dim and the lit chevrons do all the work. Crossed fine hatch that jumps is also a short walk from moiré, and it must be tested.

Two hard bars with a ragged nap crossing their edges at 0.5 s is the right contrast of textures. But a hot seam in a dark-red slab that opens and lets white floss spill out is a risk even when horizontal, which is why the essay rules out the vertical. Tack gets the same slab-and-gap with a cleaner picture and fewer sprites.

A quilt of hard-edged hair tiles that "goes from invisible to metal" and walks mint, green, blue, violet as it dies is the only idea with new colour logic and no shape at all. Each tile has its own grain, so a chord is an instantly countable patchwork, and a repeat mirrors the grain. Soft to loud goes from thread to plate, which is a real texture axis. It says iridescent more than fuzzy, and the palette must stay away from gamer RGB.

A finite stock spent one wedge per note, the picture fullest before the music starts, is a beautiful idea, and the fuzz would read instantly. But a pale dome of spokes is a dandelion, as the essay admits, and cropping it by the floor does not stop that. With `near` at 0.7 it might pass as an arc of nap, and that version should be judged instead.

No curve at all, just two straight segments and a corner, and the canvas stacking them into "a fan of straight hairlines" is a graphic find. It is cheap and fast and a run sprays well. But it comes down to thin lines, 3 px at best and 1.25 px red after, so the frame is sparse and it lives in Hammer's neighbourhood.

The sag law making 2 px of shift look alive is real looking, and a whole path lighting in one step is a good gesture. But the essay's own fear, "a dim wire diagram", is what I see: thin straight lines in a graph layout, with a Laplacian you must be told about. This has Blade's profile, a clever concept that may look like nothing.

Two opposing fans of torn dashes turning like a clock hand is a whole-screen gesture from a small share of pixels, and the fans glitter rather than slide, which is the true thing. It has more composition than the other Glint. But it looks like the highlight on a CD, a radial figure from one fixed point, chords become a thicket, and it needs care to stay clear of ring and moiré looks.

Low notes as six 76 px red discs are bolder than the other Beading, and reading register from spacing is good. But a hard cut from bar to discs loses the elastic it claims, and crescents lit "on the lower rim" are a small painting of a dewdrop. It is a dot row, not a texture.

A dark nap of needles that all turn in one step toward a spot and stop short, so "the spot itself stays black". That hole is the picture, and you would not want to put a finger there. Chords make territories with sharp borders where neighbours disagree. It sounds like a recipe but passes, because nothing travels or spawns, and only 240 triangles are needed.

The note is literally a change of texture, a hard cut from combed to crossed, and you "could read a note here with no change in brightness". This answers the user's word directly, is flat, has no bodies and no physics, and a viewer would say prickly. Pitch only moves the patch, so melody is weak, and the combed ground at 0.25 is close to the rounding limit.

A fingerprint per pitch class, so "the eye learns C", is the most learnable mapping here, and a comb with a gap keeps it from being an asterisk. But stars on a brick lattice lean decorative, near snowflakes or a wallpaper of fireworks, and the sharpness stays small at this scale.

One huge flat red thorn from the side of the frame, thinning to "under 2 px over the last 30 px". It is a Suprematist picture on every note, and concave sides are what make the eye flinch. A chord's tips aim at one point with 6 px gaps, which is the tension of the whole set. It keeps Handover's clarity, and being bright and big it avoids Blade's fault.

Razor for two steps and wool after, softness as geometry and a repeat as "fuzz to razor, in place", is the neatest answer to crisp-first in any essay. The strike is excellent. What stands on the frame afterwards is thin strips of hairline at about 25 % ember, so it is a strong event in a weak picture, and neighbouring wavy lines could still beat.

Long needles from top and bottom that miss each other, so the black zigzag between them is the picture. It is fully in on the attack step, it hurts, and repeats ratchet "24 px deeper", which fits repeated Rachmaninoff chords perfectly. It is a little close to teeth, and a driving-in motif needs a look, but straight sides and full-height spikes keep it a graphic seam.

A full-height barcode where a note makes light by crowding, "a contraction does not add stuff, it moves it", and the neighbours pay with wider gaps. It has Ikeda's severity with a body, and a viewer sees an accordion-like give. A run fusing into a held slab is true and striking. A moving comb over its own ghost is the one risk.

Thick full-width chevron bands flipping click, clack, with black diamonds opening between them, make a bold constructivist frame, and parity is a musical oddity. But it is more flag than texture, since the arms are rigid and the elastic is a brief ring at the crease. In dense music it risks wallpaper.

A flat hot sector swept out on the attack is a good shape, and rubato setting the throw is a musician's idea. But the needle visibly leans back before the note for up to a second, so there is motion with no attack. With `load = 0` it passes, and then what remains is a wiper blade, with the texture mostly gone.

Width from perimeter, so a leap pulls the band to a hair and a cluster lets it go fat, is a nice surprise you actually see. But a jumping polygon outline is thinner and less of a form than the Film sail, and a repeat changes nothing but a flash and a hum. The hum on a freed line can also drift toward trembling.

It "dies by rotation and never by fading", a solid bone sheet that reaches opaque hairlines without ever being dim. That is a beautiful, clean answer to the fade, and a repeat slams the wall shut. The full sheet is 62,400 px, just over the 6 % line, so the biggest need the HOT fallback. It may read as blinds, and pitch is only a place.

A dim rectangle falling toward the next note is anticipation, and it is, as the essay says, "one step from a karaoke bouncing ball". Height as a clock is neat for rubato, but there is no texture at all to see. The user would laugh, and the essay already offers it up first in a cull.

A note selects a contour from ground that was always there, written in hard needles, so there is a soft ribbon from across the room and sparks up close. A chromatic run walks a line across the terrain "with no motion at all", and that gestalt beats loose scatter. It could turn pretty and screensaver-like, and needles of 2 to 7 px need the full alpha they are given.

The same grains from further off is a true thought, and contraction is a fresh gesture. But 70 polygons with "one lit facet" in quartz and rust are a picture of gravel, shard-like, and that is what the user dropped in shatter. A six-note chord costs about 420 draws for 0.3 s, too heavy for the result.

Every edge at plus or minus 34 degrees and chevron stripes in flat heaps can be a hard-edge painting, like Stella in sand. A slope that "never changes" through a catastrophe is a strong rule. But a row of peaks on a floor is one bad day from a mountain range, and a soft note bringing down a heap can muddle the mapping from note to event.

A screenful of slabs from knife-edged to sugar, age counted in notes, so a still frame shows the texture range and the recent past. It takes the user's complaint about dissolves and fixes it exactly, because "between notes the picture does not change at all". It looks like a woodblock print, and it is the cheapest widget in its essay. The strike needs more than a 3 px line on two faces to carry a note in big music.

A note that adds exactly one line to a ruled field is true topology, and counting tines is a nice idea. But it is a stripe field with a jump, next to Riley and to the dropped moiré, and only a mathematician sees a dislocation at 22 px wavelength. A ground at 24 %, upscaled twice, is neither bright nor sharp.

Thick butt-ended struts up to 27 px on three lattice directions could look like a heavy constructivist diagram, and the two hands pressing toward each other is a real musical picture. Nothing moves and the stiffness comes across. But a branching bright path from an edge is what chord lightning was, and it stays out only if the struts stay thick and the branching low.

The repeat that pulls loosened fuzz back to a hairline is a great moment, and one chord, one figure is musical. But a Chladni pattern in dots is a mathematical screensaver, the Whitney ghost the essay names. At 4,000 to 5,600 rects it is also the heaviest idea in the set.

A harp comb of horizontal needles and a dust tuft that marks "where the needle no longer is" gives two textures with a gap between them, and a rising run as a staircase of clouds would look good. But the tines are 1.5 px at 35 % and clouds are small, so the picture is delicate rather than strong. The dust also risks looking like a soft smudge from a distance.

clusters.why: All three light fixed marks with no motion. 1:glint and 3:mica both make pitch class an angle, and 3:mica beats 1:glint because big clumped shards read from afar and a repeat is the same constellation. 8:mica beats both on the eye, because the marks close into a contour line and so the frame has a form, while the other two are scatter.

Both select a figure out of fixed dashes by angle. The bow-tie is a bigger gesture, but it always pivots on one point, looks like a CD highlight and tangles on chords. The ribbons roam a geography and stay separate.

Same Plateau-Rayleigh law. 4 keeps the visible necking, so the elastic exists for a moment, stays flat and adds the surprise that loud means fewer. 6 cuts straight to discs and adds dew-drop crescents, which is more literal, though its 76 px red low beads are bolder and worth borrowing.

Same one-plane idea, same dark slab. 3 has continuous pitch, leaves that thin where the melody lives, end faces that flash, and motion designed around the canvas ghost, so the frame gets richer. 1 is limited to 12 seams and small slips, and its flat hexagon changes little.

Both rest on a line that stops at what is older. Stop Dead's three angles, tapered wedges and two kinds of end have a signature of their own. T-joints has the better colour, a flash that is a whole cell, but it lands on the familiar Mondrian subdivision. Borrow the lit cell if Stop Dead looks dim.

Both write age in the edge, with corners going first. Sublimate has the harder strike and the more dangerous shape, but its rounding runs between notes. Cut changes only on attacks, keeps a full range of edges on screen, and gives fuzz from hard grains. If the Cut strike is too small, take Sublimate's bone outline.

Both bake a full-frame coat and clip a noisy patch. Bristle changes direction only, with no shaking, so the texture is the entire event and there is nothing trembling for the user to dislike. Twitch's shear seam is lovely but comes with a shaking hide.
Both raise hair on a note and lay it down by rotation. Furred puts it on a hard form and gets a picture and a real fur read. Hackles has a meter on a thin line.

Both open a dark-red slab on a second material. Tack's fibres are tension that fails at random, so the texture is the event and it is over in 0.35 s. Suture's floss stays longer, but it spills from a slit, costs more sprites and is riskier for suggestiveness.

All are a straight mark becoming a curl. Snapweed's whole mark turns to a big coil by arc-length, so it has the biggest picture and a true point. Snapback is a close second, with hand-like scribbles that are thinner. Peel's 14 px scroll is an ornament on a strip.

Both are one closed form whose corners are the last few notes. Film is a filled mass with scooped edges and needles, so it reads as tension and as a picture at once. Sinew's thin-when-stretched band is good but is a jumping outline.

All three show something before the note because `CHORDS` allows it, and all break no fake attacks to a degree. Only Latch can drop the wind-up and keep a shape (the swept sector), so it is the only one that survives the filter, though weakened. Neck is the best thought but the worst for suggestiveness, and Hop is a toy.

All make a note take something away. Knap is the only one that is flat, abstract and turns repeats into a sharper form, provided its near-black default is replaced. Clock is a dandelion, Unzip is suggestive, and Flinch is a dim field of holes.

Both are huge sharp triangles entering from outside the frame and cutting a black gap by near-miss. Prickle has the concave profile and fills the frame with one form per note. Interlock counts better and handles repeats better, so it is worth keeping as a distinct widget.

All stack countable layers as a record. Beds has colour and the tilted unconformity, which is the best single still. Needle ice has the best rhythm and is second. Repose is handsome but looks most like a landscape.

All give a pitch a fixed address on a lattice. Sheen's tiles have area, grain and colour, so a chord is seen as a patchwork at once. Areole's stars are better for learning a note by eye but look decorative, and Causeway is dim.

All are thin struck lines that are not Hammer. Crimp's change of texture is visible at any distance and answers the brief's main word. Pluck's corner is the more surprising shape but thinner, and Catkin depends on faint clouds.

overall: The set gets the hard part right: nearly every idea appears whole on the attack, moves nothing between notes, and has done its homework on the real thing, so the fake-attack and travelling-front traps are mostly avoided. Where it wins is flat, big, single decisions you can see on a still frame: a concave thorn, a scooped sail, a pile that lies the other way, an empty spot ringed by points. It keeps getting three things wrong. Too many ideas are beautiful physics that has to be explained (Laplacians, dislocations, contact time, curvature), which is how Blade died. Too many rest at T 0.2 to 0.35 in hairlines or near-black on black, so they look like nothing after the flash. And almost everything is bone over oxblood, inherited from last night, so the eye gets one palette; the few that escape it (Film's blue, Sheen's mint to violet, Underbark's orange) stand out at once. Fuzzy is the most under-delivered word, since many claimed fuzz is really a flash of hairs, while Nap, Bristle and Furred actually deliver it.
